title: Agent Lifespan Management
summary: Control how agent instances are created, leased, reused, drained, and retired so long-running work does not accumulate abandoned resources or authority.
overview: Agent lifespan management governs the operational lifetime of an execution instance and its associated resources. These resources can include worker slots, browser sessions, tool connections, temporary artifacts, credentials, and memory. A durable conversation or task can outlive any particular process; the process should not become the sole owner of its business state.

Choose deliberately between short-lived workers and reusable sessions. Reuse can reduce initialization cost but increases contamination and leakage risks. Lease ownership, explicit cleanup, and terminal-state handling ensure that abandoned clients or failed workers do not leave active agents consuming capacity indefinitely.

production.poc: A prototype often creates an agent for each request and relies on process exit for cleanup. Inventory every resource that actually survives completion.
production.production: Production defines creation limits, idle expiry, maximum runtime, cancellation, and cleanup ownership. Credentials should expire independently of whether cleanup succeeds.
production.scale: At scale, workers need graceful draining during deployments and controllers must reclaim orphaned leases. Measure live instances against active business operations to detect silent resource accumulation before capacity exhaustion.

components.name: Instance manager
components.role: Creates and tracks agent instances under tenant and capability quotas.

components.name: Lease service
components.role: Assigns renewable ownership and fences expired workers from further writes.

components.name: Resource registry
components.role: Records sessions, connections, temporary objects, and credentials associated with each run.

components.name: Drain controller
components.role: Stops new assignments while allowing bounded in-flight work to finish or checkpoint.

components.name: Reaper
components.role: Detects expired, abandoned, or terminal instances and performs retryable cleanup.

flow.title: Allocate instance
flow.description: Check quotas and register the run, owner, maximum age, and resource budget.

flow.title: Acquire resources
flow.description: Create only necessary sessions and attach them to the resource registry.

flow.title: Renew ownership
flow.description: Heartbeat the lease while checking cancellation, idle timeout, and parent task status.

flow.title: Checkpoint or drain
flow.description: Save progress before deployment, lease handoff, or graceful termination.

flow.title: Finalize task
flow.description: Commit terminal business status before releasing resources and revoking capabilities.

flow.title: Reap leftovers
flow.description: Reconcile expired leases and cleanup failures using an independent controller.

diagrams.title: Instance lifecycle and orphan recovery
diagrams.code:
stateDiagram-v2
 [*] --> Allocated
 Allocated --> Running: Lease acquired
 Running --> Idle: Waiting without active work
 Idle --> Running: New permitted work
 Running --> Draining: Deployment or shutdown
 Draining --> Checkpointed: Progress saved
 Checkpointed --> Released: Resources closed
 Running --> Expired: Lease lost
 Idle --> Expired: Idle limit reached
 Expired --> Reaping: Independent cleanup
 Reaping --> Released: Cleanup verified
 Released --> [*]
diagrams.caption: Business progress is checkpointed before resource release, and an independent reaper handles lost workers.

useCase.title: Managing browser-assisted reconciliation agents
useCase.situation: A finance platform uses browser automation to reconcile supplier portals that lack stable machine interfaces.
useCase.problem: Abandoned browser sessions retain cookies and consume memory after users close their dashboards or tasks fail.
useCase.requirement: The assistant must preserve reconciliation progress while bounding session lifetime and access to external accounts.
useCase.architecture: An instance manager leases browser workers, tracks their resources, and hands completed checkpoints to durable storage.
runtime: A reconciliation request receives a bounded session; the worker renews its lease only while actively progressing.
During deployment, workers stop accepting jobs, checkpoint remaining portal positions, and close browser resources before replacement.
useCase.failure: If a worker disappears, its lease expires and the reaper closes remaining sessions while a new worker resumes from durable state.
useCase.impact: Track orphaned sessions, memory per active run, cleanup latency, credential age, and drain completion before increasing concurrency.

tradeoffs.benefit: Cleanup and tenant separation are easier to reason about.
Expensive browser or tool setup can be amortized.
tradeoffs.cost: State contamination and resource leakage become more likely.
Shutdown takes longer and needs a hard upper bound.

failures.scenario: A worker keeps running after losing its lease
failures.detection: Fencing checks reject writes from the old ownership version.
failures.recovery: Stop the worker and reconcile any external actions.

failures.detection: Resource registry retains unreleased objects past their deadline.
failures.recovery: Retry independently and alert with resource ownership details.

mistakes.mistake: Equating process lifetime with task lifetime
mistakes.fix: Persist business state separately from worker resources.

mistakes.mistake: Keeping credentials alive until cleanup succeeds
mistakes.fix: Use short-lived scoped credentials with independent expiry.
Isolate sessions and clear all state before any permitted reuse.

whenToUse: Agents hold expensive or sensitive resources over time.
Deployments must preserve long-running task progress.
Concurrency and orphan cleanup need explicit control.
whenNotToUse: Stateless function execution already provides adequate lifecycle guarantees.
There are no retained resources or long-running sessions.
Reuse adds complexity without measurable startup savings.
checklist: Inventory all resources owned by a run.
Set idle and absolute lifetime limits.
Monitor resources after terminal task completion.
